newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hopes new CIA nominee avoids conflict.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hopes new CIA nominee avoids conflict.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday deplored the "inexusably flawed" political process that forced Tony Lake to withdraw as President Bill Clinton's nominee for CIA director but said Clinton had plunged into the search for a replacement.

Acting CIA Director George Tenet led the early speculation and drew a tentative favourable comment from Senate Republican Majority Leader Trent Lott, who said, "Barring something I don't know about, it looks like he would be a good choice."

"We will want to move quickly," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters as he blasted the Senate's handling of Lake's confirmation. "I think that the president feels that the process that Tony went through was inexcusably flawed."
Lake told Democrat Clinton on Monday night that he felt he had become a political football and was withdrawing from bruising confirmation hearings in the Republican-led Senate.

White House officials insisted Clinton had tried to talk him out of the decision and promised to back him indefinitely if he stood and fought. They rejected suggestions Clinton, notorious for fumbled nominations, had left Lake hanging.

"I think there's been no question about the commitment of ... this president to Tony's confirmation," Samuel Berger, Lake's successor as Clinton's national security adviser told reporters who questioned the president's support of Lake.
"The president believes very, very deeply today no less than the day he made the selection that Tony was the right person to lead the CIA."

Lake said he feared the agency and his own integrity would be damaged by a prolonged pounding from Republican senators on issues ranging from his knowledge of questionable White House fund-raising practices to his failure to divest himself of some stock and U.S. policy in Bosnia.
Sen. Richard Shelby, chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and Lake's leading antagonist, insisted he "ran a fair hearing," and added, "I was never out to get Mr. Lake."
He said his tough scrutiny was driven by a desire to confirm that "proper person for this very important job."
The Democratic vice-chairman of the committee, Sen. Robert Kerrey of Nebraska, strongly disagreed. "I do not believe the ... process that Tony Lake went through was fair," he said.
"I think we've got to be careful that whoever's sent up here gets due process, a reasonable hearing."

The early betting line on replacements focused on Tenet, who has been acting agency director pending Lake's expected arrival. He has already gone through the rigours of winning Senate confirmation as the CIA's deputy director.

Republican leader Lott told reporters he had talked with White House officials on the issue and Tenet was "one of the ones I have the impression they are considering ... It is clear to me they are working aggressively."
"I am not promoting him," Lott added. "It is one of the names that has been mentioned."

Officials said another person under consideration was Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, who is leaving the Justice Department but who is known as a strong administrator and who has not announced what she planned to do next.
Another name mentioned was Frank Wisner, the U.S. ambassador to India and son of one of the CIA's founders and most celebrated intelligence officers.
Clinton has had a star-crossed history when it comes to choices for director of central intelligence. His next choice will be his fifth nominee for the post in as many years.
"We certainly don't want to go through this again, and neither does the president," said one senior official who had tried to help Lake through the confirmation process.

Lake, 57, was nominated to succeed John Deutch, who left in December. Lake condemned the confirmation process as "nasty and brutish but not short," a play on a famous aphorism about primitive life by philosopher Thomas Hobbes.

Lake's withdrawal surprised many who had predicted his eventual confirmation and said he handled himself well during last week's often testy Senate hearings. The panel had been set to resume hearings on his nomination on Tuesday.
